correctness.rationale: Exact Gaussian centering makes the sample mean independent of the centered design. Frisch–Waugh–Lovell gives each quadratic slope as a residual-numerator divided by chi-squared radial magnitude. The upper q-moment bound is equivalent to E[\(\chi_{n-d}^{-q}\)]<infinity. For every nonzero quadratic matrix, an explicit centered three-coordinate witness forces a nonzero first-order numerator on an open set; the radial integral diverges exactly at \(q\ge n-d\), with the Gaussian independent sample mean transferring the divergence to the OLS intercept. Its other terms have all polynomial moments. Bias and exact finite-risk identities follow by independent Gaussian/Wishart moments; the \(d=1\) exception uses a separate bounded ratio and sixth spherical moments. 509 exact symbolic/rational checker assertions passed, but the infinite-family statement relies on proof, not checks.

value.rationale: This determines a natural complete finite-sample boundary for a widely used numerical integration method, not an arbitrary slice: at one sample above the number of controls even the fitted-intercept mean fails, at two samples above it MSE fails, and only at three above it becomes finite, despite the base Monte Carlo estimator having all moments. Exact \(d=1\) exception, arbitrary quadratic matrix necessity and geometric residual-rank mechanism make the result structurally informative. It suggests concrete risks of near-interpolating same-sample control fitting without claiming a new universal algorithm.
